en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Defeats (Pārājikakaṇḍa)
3. The Third Pārājika Training Rule At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was teaching a discourse on foulness to the bhikkhus in many ways, [explaining] foulness...
He speaks in praise of it; he speaks in praise of the development of the foul; he speaks repeatedly in praise of the attainment of the foul.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, I wish to dwell in seclusion for half a month."
"No one should approach me, except for a single person bringing almsfood.
"Very well, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One, and indeed no one approached the Blessed One except for a single person bringing almsfood.

The monks thought: "The Blessed One has spoken on the theme of foulness in many ways; he has praised foulness, he has praised the development of foulness, and he has repeatedly praised the attainment of foulness."
They dwell devoted to the practice of the meditation on the foul in its many aspects and variations.
They are repelled by, ashamed of, and disgusted with their own bodies.

Just as a woman or a man—youthful, young, fond of adornment, and freshly bathed—would be repelled, ashamed, and disgusted if a snake’s carcass, a dog’s carcass, or a human carcass were hung around their neck, so too do they feel such revulsion toward their own bodies.
In the same way, those bhikkhus, being terrified, humiliated, and disgusted by their own bodies,
deprive themselves of life and deprive one another of life as well;
they even approach Migalaṇḍika, that sham ascetic, and speak thus:
“Please, friend, deprive us of life;
this bowl and robe shall be yours.
Then Migalaṇḍika the ascetic fraud, having been hired for the bowl and robe, killed several bhikkhus and, taking his blood-stained sword, went to the river Vaggumudā.
Then, as Migalaṇḍika the sham ascetic was washing that bloody sword, remorse arose within him and he felt regret:
"It is a loss for me, truly a loss; it is ill-gotten for me, truly not well-gotten.
Indeed, I have produced much demerit, in that I have deprived virtuous monks of noble character of their lives."
Then a certain deity from the host of Māra, coming through the water without breaking the surface, said this to Migalaṇḍika the ascetic hypocrite:
"Excellent, excellent, worthy man! It is a gain for you, worthy man; it is well-gained by you, worthy man.
Much merit has been produced by you, worthy man, in that you have ferried across those who had not crossed."
Then Migalaṇḍika, the fake ascetic— thinking,
"It is indeed a gain for me, it is indeed well-obtained by me, much merit has indeed been produced by me, for I am indeed ferrying across those who have not crossed"—
took a sharp sword and, approaching from monastery to monastery and from cell to cell, spoke thus:
“Who has not crossed over? Whom shall I ferry across?
At that time, those monks who were not free from lust felt fear, trepidation, and horripilation;
however, those monks who were free from lust felt no fear, no trepidation, and no horripilation.
Then Migalaṇḍika the false ascetic deprived one bhikkhu of life in a single day; he deprived two bhikkhus of life in a single day;
he deprived three bhikkhus of life in a single day; he deprived four bhikkhus of life in a single day;
he deprived five bhikkhus of life in a single day; he deprived ten [bhikkhus]...
He deprived one bhikkhu of life in a single day; he deprived twenty bhikkhus of life in a single day;
he deprived thirty bhikkhus of life in a single day; he deprived forty bhikkhus of life in a single day;
he deprived fifty bhikkhus of life in a single day; he deprived sixty bhikkhus of life in a single day.
Then, at the end of that half-month, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, why is it that the Saṅgha of bhikkhus appears as if diminished?
“It is because, Bhante, the Blessed One has been teaching the discourse on foulness to the bhikkhus in many ways.”
He speaks in praise of foulness; he speaks in praise of the development of foulness; he speaks in praise, time and again, of the attainment of foulness.
And those monks, venerable sir, [think]: “The Blessed One indeed speaks on foulness in many ways;
he speaks in praise of foulness; he speaks in praise of the development of foulness; he speaks in praise, time and again, of the attainment of foulness.”
‘[The body] speaks,’ they dwell devoted to the practice of meditation on foulness in its many aspects and variations.
They are repelled by, ashamed of, and disgusted with their own bodies.

Just as a woman or a man—young, youthful, and fond of adornment—having washed their head, would be repelled, ashamed, and disgusted if a snake’s carcass, a dog’s carcass, or a human carcass were hung around their neck, so too do they feel such revulsion.
In the same way, those bhikkhus, being terrified, humiliated, and disgusted by their own bodies,
deprive themselves of life and deprive one another of life as well;
they even approach Migalaṇḍika, that sham ascetic, and speak thus:
“‘It would be well for you, friend, to deprive us of life;
this bowl and robe shall be yours.

Then, Bhante, Migalaṇḍika the false ascetic, having been hired with a bowl and robe, deprived one bhikkhu of life in a single day … [and so on] … he even deprived sixty bhikkhus of life in a single day.”
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would explain another method so that this Saṅgha of bhikkhus might be established in final knowledge.
“In that case, Ānanda, assemble all the bhikkhus who dwell in dependence on Vesālī in the assembly hall.
“Yes, Bhante,” he replied.
Having assented to the Blessed One, the Venerable Ānanda gathered together all the monks who were dwelling in dependence on Vesālī in the assembly hall; having approached the Blessed One,
he said this to him:
“Venerable sir, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has assembled;
now, venerable sir, let the Blessed One do as he deems timely.
Then the Blessed One went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:

“Monks, this concentration through mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is peaceful and sublime, an unadulterated state of happiness, and it causes whatever evil, unwholesome states that have arisen to vanish on the spot and to subside.

Just as, monks, in the last month of summer, the dust and dirt stirred up by the wind are caused to vanish on the spot and subside by a great, untimely rain cloud; even so, monks, this concentration through mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is peaceful and sublime, an unadulterated state of happiness, and it causes whatever evil, unwholesome states that have arisen to vanish on the spot and to subside.”

In the same way, monks, when concentration through mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated, it is peaceful, sublime, unadulterated, and pleasant—a dwelling that causes whatever evil, unwholesome states that have arisen to vanish on the spot and to be stilled.
And how, monks, is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed? How is it cultivated so that it is peaceful and sublime?
And what is that unsurpassed, blissful dwelling which, as each evil, unwholesome state arises, causes it to vanish on the spot and brings it to pacification?
Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Mindfully he breathes in; mindfully he breathes out.
Breathing in long, he understands: "I am breathing in long"; or breathing out long, he understands:
"I am breathing out long. Breathing in short, he understands: "I am breathing in short"; or breathing out short, he understands:
"I am breathing out short. He trains thus: "Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in"; he trains thus: "Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out."
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in experiencing rapture"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out experiencing rapture.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure."
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formations"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formations.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in tranquilizing the mental formations"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out tranquilizing the mental formations.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in experiencing the mind"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out experiencing the mind."
Gladdening the mind …pe… concentrating the mind …pe… liberating the mind …pe…
Contemplating impermanence … [and so on] … contemplating dispassion … [and so on] … contemplating cessation … [and so on] …
“He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.
Monks, when concentration through mindfulness of breathing is developed and cultivated in this way, it is peaceful and sublime, an unadulterated state of blissful living;
and it causes whatever evil, unwholesome states that have arisen to disappear on the spot and to be stilled.”
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having assembled the community of monks, questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that monks have themselves deprived themselves of life, that they have deprived one another of life, and that they have approached Migalaṇḍika, that sham ascetic, and said:
‘It would be good for us, friend, if you were to deprive us of life; this bowl and robe shall be yours’?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“Monks, it is unbecoming for those monks, it is unsuitable, it is unworthy, it is unbecoming of a recluse, it is improper, and it is not to be done.
“How indeed, monks, could those bhikkhus deprive themselves of life, or deprive one another of life, or even approach Migalaṇḍika, that fake ascetic, and say:
‘It would be good, friend, if you were to deprive us of life; this robe and bowl shall be yours’?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on].”
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whatever monk should intentionally deprive a human being of life, or should seek an instrument for him,
he too is one who has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.”
Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, a certain lay follower was ill;
his wife was beautiful, lovely to behold, and inspiring.
The group-of-six monks were infatuated with that woman.
Then it occurred to the group-of-six monks:
"Friends, if that lay follower continues to live, we shall not obtain that woman."
"Come now, friends, let us praise death to that lay follower.
Then the group of six bhikkhus went to where that lay follower was; having approached, they said this to him:

"Lay follower, you have performed what is beautiful, you have performed what is wholesome, you have provided a refuge for those who are afraid; you have not committed evil, you have not been cruel, you have not done anything blameworthy."
You have done what is good; you have not done what is evil.
What is the use to you of this wretched, miserable life?
Death is better for you than life.
“After you have passed away from here, with the breakup of the body, after death, you will be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
There, endowed and possessed of the fivefold divine cords of sensual pleasure, you will enjoy yourself.
Then that lay follower—
“The noble ladies have indeed spoken the truth.
For I have performed what is beautiful, performed what is wholesome, and provided a refuge for the fearful; I have not committed evil, nor acted with cruelty, nor committed any transgression.
I have done what is beautiful; I have not done what is evil.”
"What is the use of this wretched and miserable life for me?
Death is better for me than life.
Having passed away from here, at the breaking up of the body after death, I shall be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world."
Therein, thinking, “I shall sport, provided and endowed with the fivefold divine strands of sensual pleasure,” he ate foods that were unwholesome,
chewed edibles that were unwholesome, tasted delicacies that were unwholesome, and drank drinks that were unwholesome. As he was eating foods that were unwholesome,
chewing edibles that were unwholesome, tasting delicacies that were unwholesome, and drinking drinks that were unwholesome, a severe illness arose in him.
He passed away from that very illness.
His wife complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"These Sakyan-son ascetics are shameless, immoral, and liars."
"These people indeed claim to be practitioners of the Dhamma, practitioners of equanimity, practitioners of the holy life, speakers of truth, virtuous, and of noble character.
Yet they possess neither the state of a recluse nor the state of a brahmin;

their state of a recluse is lost, their state of a brahmin is lost. Where is their state of a recluse? Where is their state of a brahmin? They have departed from the state of a recluse; they have departed from the state of a brahmin."
"These people have praised death to my husband;
it was by them that my husband was killed.
Other people also complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying: [as above].
“Shameless are these recluses, sons of the Sakyans; they are immoral and speakers of falsehood.
Yet they claim to be practitioners of the Dhamma, practitioners of integrity, practitioners of the holy life, speakers of truth, virtuous, and of beautiful character.
They possess neither the state of a recluse nor the state of a brahmin; their state of a recluse is lost, their state of a brahmin is lost.”

For these there is no state of a recluse; whence could there be for them the state of a recluse? Whence could there be for them the state of a brahmin? These have departed from the state of a recluse;
these have departed from the state of a brahmin.
These have praised the beauty of death for this lay follower.
“By these [means], the lay follower has been killed.
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those monks who were of few desires... they grumbled, complained, and criticized:
“How indeed can the group-of-six monks praise death to a lay follower?
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, monks, that you praised death to a lay follower?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“It is unseemly, foolish men, it is unbecoming, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.”
“How indeed, you foolish men, can you praise death to a lay follower?
This, foolish men, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:”
“Whatever monk should intentionally deprive a human being of life, or seek a weapon for him, or praise the beauty of death, or incite him toward death, saying:
‘O man, what is this wretched, miserable life to you?

Death is better for you than life,’ thus with a mind intent on death, with a resolve for death, in many ways praising the beauty of death or inciting him toward death—[this is an offense entailing expulsion].”
“This too is one who has committed a defeat and is no longer in communion.
As for “whoever,” whoever of such a kind... [and so forth].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Intentionally" (sañcicca):
Transgression occurs when one knows, perceives, intends, and resolves [to act].
What is called "human form" (manussaviggaha) refers to that which,
from the first arising of mind and the first manifestation of consciousness in the mother's womb until the time of death— within this interval— is called human form.
"Should deprive of life" means:
one cuts off, obstructs, and disrupts the continuity of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
Or, "one should seek out an executioner for him."
"A sword, or a spear, or a javelin, or a club, or a stone, or a weapon, or poison, or a rope.
"He would praise death" means he shows the disadvantage in living and speaks in praise of death.
"Or incites [another] to death" means:
"Take up a weapon," or "Eat poison," or "Hang yourself with a rope and die.
"O man! [he says].
This is a term of address:
"What is the use of this evil, wretched life?"—
thus, it is called an "evil life."
Compared to the life of the wealthy, the life of the poor is wretched and miserable;
compared to the life of those with wealth, the life of those without wealth is wretched;
compared to the life of the gods, the life of human beings is wretched.

A "wretched life" refers to one whose hand is cut off, whose foot is cut off, whose hands and feet are cut off, whose ear is cut off, whose nose is cut off, or whose ears and nose are cut off; thinking,
"Death is better for you than this evil and this wretched life."
Thus, "mind and intellect":
that which is mind is intellect, and that which is intellect is mind. "Volition of mind."
One who perceives death, whose intention is death, and whose purpose is death.
"In many ways" means by various high and low modes.
"Or he would praise death" means he shows the disadvantage in living and speaks in praise of death, saying:
"When you have passed away from here, with the breakup of the body, after death, you will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world."
"There you shall sport, endowed and possessed of the fivefold divine sense-pleasures.
Or, "He may incite one to death" means:
"Take up a weapon, eat poison, hang yourself with a rope and die, or throw yourself into a pit, a chasm, or a precipice."
This too is said with reference to the preceding [offense].
"He becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense" means:
Just as a large stone, once split in two, cannot be joined back together, even so a bhikkhu who intentionally deprives a human being of life is no longer a samaṇa, no longer a son of the Sakyans.
Therefore it is said: "He is one who has committed a pārājika offense."
"Non-residence":
residence means performing formal acts together, reciting the scriptures together, and being subject to the same training—this is what is called "residence.
That [person] does not have that [residence] with him; therefore, he is called one who is "not in communion."
In person, by formal resolution, by messenger, by a succession of messengers, by a messenger who has been sent back, by a messenger who has gone and returned,
one who is alone but perceives another as being alone, or one who is not alone but perceives another as being alone.
Perceiving one who is not worthy of gifts as worthy of gifts, and perceiving one who is worthy of gifts as worthy of gifts,
he praises them with the body.
He praises with speech;
he praises with both body and speech;
he praises by means of a messenger.
One praises by means of a letter:
a trench, a parapet, placing near, medicine, the offering of visible forms, the offering of sounds, the offering of odors,
the offering of tastes, the offering of tangibles, the offering of mental phenomena, pointing out, instruction, making a sign, and making a gesture.
One kills a neighbor oneself by means of the body, or by means of something connected to the body, or by means of something relinquishable.
"Having resolved" means...
Having made a resolution, he commands: “Pierce him thus! Strike him thus! Kill him thus!
A bhikkhu commands another bhikkhu: “Kill so-and-so,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If that person, thinking it is that [other] person, deprives that person of life, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika) for both.
A bhikkhu commands another bhikkhu: “Kill so-and-so,” he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, thinking it was that person, he kills someone else, there is no offense for the one who gave the order; the killer commits an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
A bhikkhu commands another bhikkhu: “Kill so-and-so,” he commits an offense of wrong-doing.
If, thinking it is someone else, he deprives that person of life, there is an offense of defeat for both.
If a monk commands another monk, saying, "Deprive so-and-so of life," there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If, thinking it is someone else, he deprives another of life, there is no offense for the one who gave the order, but there is an offense of defeat for the murderer.
If a bhikkhu commands another bhikkhu, saying, “Tell so-and-so: ‘Let so-and-so tell so-and-so: Let so-and-so deprive so-and-so of life,’” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When he informs the other person, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
When the murderer accepts the task, there is a serious offense (thullaccaya) for the one who instigated it.
If he deprives him of life, there is an offense of *pārājika* for all [involved].
If a monk commands another monk, saying, “Tell so-and-so: ‘Let so-and-so tell so-and-so: Let so-and-so deprive so-and-so of life,’” there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If he commands someone else, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
The executioner accepts [the order]; there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he deprives that person of life, there is no offense for the one who was at the root [of the instigation];
however, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) for both the commander and the executioner.
A bhikkhu commands another bhikkhu: “Kill so-and-so,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
He goes and then returns, saying: “I am not able to deprive him of life.
He commands him again: “When you are able, then deprive him of life,” there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he thus deprives him of life, there is an offense of *pārājika* for both.
If a monk commands another monk, saying, "Deprive so-and-so of life," there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
Having given the command, if he feels remorse and does not inform [the other], saying, "Do not kill him," [there is no offense].
If he deprives him of life, there is an offense of defeat for both.
If a monk commands another monk, saying, "Kill so-and-so," there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Having given the command, if he feels remorse and says, "Do not kill him," [the situation changes].

Thus—"I have been commanded by you"—he deprives that person of life; there is no offense for the one who was the original instigator (*mūlaṭṭha*), but there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) for the murderer.
A monk commands another monk: "Deprive such-and-such a person of life"; there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Having given the command, he becomes remorseful and says: "Do not kill him."
Thinking, “Very well,” he desists; there is no offense for either of them.
If one who is innocent, perceiving another as innocent, says, “Oh, may so-and-so be killed!”, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If one who is not worthy of death speaks in private with the perception that he is worthy of death, saying, "Oh, may such-and-such a person be killed," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). [Likewise for] one who is not worthy of death,
perceiving him as worthy of death.
If one says aloud, “Oh, may such-and-such a person be killed,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If one speaks in private,
perceiving it to be in private,
saying, “Oh, may such-and-such a person be killed,” there is an offense of wrong-doing.
“He praises with the body” means he makes a gesture with the body, saying:
“Whoever dies in this way will obtain wealth, or obtain fame, or go to heaven. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, because of that praise, [the person] experiences painful feeling thinking, “I shall die,” there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
“Marati”: there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
To “praise by speech” means to say by speech:
“Whoever dies in this way gains wealth, or gains fame, or goes to heaven”; there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, by that praise, she produces a painful sensation with the thought, "I shall die," it is a *thullaccaya* offense.
If she dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
To "praise" means to do so by means of body or speech.

If one causes a transformation by means of the body and speaks with the voice, saying, "Whoever dies in this manner will obtain wealth, or obtain fame, or go to heaven," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, through that praise, [the person] thinks, "I shall die," and gives rise to painful sensation, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If they die, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
“He praises by means of a messenger” means he announces a messenger’s message:
“Whoever dies in this way gains wealth, or gains fame, or goes to heaven. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Having heard the messenger’s message, if she inflicts painful sensation [upon herself] thinking, “I shall die,” there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
“Marati,” there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
To “commend by means of writing” means to carve a writing:
“Whoever dies thus will obtain wealth, or obtain fame, or go to heaven. For every single syllable, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Upon seeing the letter, if she gives rise to a painful sensation, thinking, "I shall die," there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
If she dies, there is an offense of *pārājika*.
[Regarding] "a pit":
If one digs a pit intending it for a human being, thinking, "He will fall in and die," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When he falls in and painful feeling arises, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If he dies, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
One digs a pit without aiming at anyone, thinking, “Whoever falls in will die”: there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If a human being falls into it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
When the person has fallen and painful sensation arises, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
Marati, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If a yakkha, a peta, or a being belonging to the animal realm who has the appearance of a human falls into it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, once it has fallen, painful sensation arises, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Marati, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If an animal falls into it, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
When it has fallen and painful sensation arises, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
Marati, there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
Regarding "reclining support" (apassena):

if one places a weapon on a reclining support, or smears it with poison, or makes it weak, or places it in a pit, a chasm, or a precipice, thinking, "By falling, he will die," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If painful feeling arises through a weapon, poison, or by falling [into a pit], there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If he dies, there is an offense of pārājika.
"Placing near" means:
If one places a sword, or a spear, or a javelin, or a club, or a stone, or a weapon, or poison, or a rope nearby, thinking, “By this he shall die,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If, thinking, “By that I shall die,” one inflicts painful sensation, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*).
If he dies, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
“Medicine” means:
if one gives ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, or molasses with the thought, “Having tasted this, he will die,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When he tastes it and painful feeling arises, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
Marati, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).

"Offering a form" means she presents an unpleasant form that is terrifying and fearsome, thinking, "Having seen this and being struck with fear, he will die"; there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, having seen him, she becomes terrified, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If he dies, there is an offense of pārājika.
If she presents an attractive form with the thought, "Having seen this, he will wither away from lack of gain and die," there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
Seeing this, if he withers away due to lack of gain, it is an offense of thullaccaya.
If he dies, it is an offense of pārājika.
This is called "the instigation by sound."
If one produces an unpleasant sound that is terrifying and fearsome, thinking, "Having heard this, he will be terrified and die," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, upon hearing it, he becomes terrified, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If he dies, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).

If he provides a pleasing sound—one that is lovely and heart-stirring—with the thought, "Having heard this, he will wither away from lack of gain and die," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If, having heard it, he withers away from lack of gain, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*).
If he dies, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).

“Offering a foul odor” means one provides an unpleasant smell that is loathsome and repulsive with the thought, “Having smelled this, she will die from loathing and repulsion”; there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When she smells it and loathing and repulsion arise, and painful feelings occur, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
Marati, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
If she provides a pleasing fragrance with the thought, "Having smelled this, he will wither from lack of food and die," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, having smelled it, he withers from lack of food, there is a serious offense (thullaccaya).
Marati, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).

"Offering a taste" means one offers a disagreeable taste that is loathsome and repulsive, thinking, "Having tasted this, he will die from loathing and repulsion"; there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, out of loathing and repulsion, she causes him to taste it and painful feelings arise, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If he dies, there is an offense of pārājika.
If she provides a pleasant-tasting substance [thinking], "Having tasted this, he will wither away for lack of food and die," there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
Having tasted it, if he dries up because he receives nothing, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
If he dies, there is an offense of pārājika.
This is called the assault by touch.
If one provides an unpleasant tactile object—a painful touch or a harsh touch—with the intention, "Touched by this, he will die," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If, touched by it, a painful feeling arises in him, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*).
If he dies, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).

If he provides a pleasant tactile object—a soft touch that is pleasant to the skin—with the thought, "Touched by this, the recipient will wither away from lack of gain and die," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If the recipient, touched by it, withers away from lack of gain, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*).
If he dies, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
Regarding "Dhammūpahāra" (the instigation of fear):
if one tells a hell-being a story about hell with the thought, "Having heard this and become terrified, he will die," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If, having heard it, he becomes terrified, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*).
Marati, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If one speaks of the heavenly realms to someone performing a meritorious deed, thinking, "Having heard this, he will die intent upon it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, having heard that, he thinks, "I shall die intent upon it," and gives rise to painful feeling, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
Marati, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
"Explaining" means that when asked, one says: "Die in this way; whoever dies in this way will obtain wealth, or obtain fame, or go to heaven"—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By that declaration, if she produces a painful sensation [thinking], "I shall die," it is a *thullaccaya* offense.
If she dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
This is called "instruction."
If, when not asked, he says: “Die in this way! Whoever dies in this way will obtain wealth, or obtain fame, or go to heaven,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If, by that instruction, [the person] thinking “I shall die,” gives rise to painful feeling, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If they die, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
Making a signal means making an appointment before a meal, after a meal, at night, or by day, saying: "By that signal, you should deprive him of life. There is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one deprives him of life by that signal, there is an offense entailing expulsion for both.
If one deprives that person of life either before or after that signal, there is no offense for the instigator; there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) for the murderer.
"Making a sign" means making a sign such as:
"I will scratch my eye, or I will raise my eyebrow, or I will raise my head; by that sign, deprive him of life. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one deprives that person of life by means of that sign, there is an offense of defeat for both.
If one deprives that person of life either before or after that sign, there is no offense for the instigator, but there is an offense of defeat for the killer.
There is no offense—
For one who acts unintentionally, unknowingly,
and without the intention for death.

Another bhikkhu, with the intention of killing him, struck that bhikkhu.
That bhikkhu died... [as before]...
That bhikkhu did not die.
He felt remorse... [as before] ...
"There is no offense, bhikkhu, of a pārājika."
“There is an offense of thullaccaya.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was giving a discourse on heaven regarding a man of wholesome deeds.
He died while absorbed in that thought.
He felt remorse... [as before] ...
"There is no offense, monk, for one who does not intend death.
Now at that time, a certain monk, intending death, spoke to a person of wholesome karma about the heavenly realms.
Intent upon that, he passed away;
[and so on] … intent upon that, he did not pass away.
He became anxious … [and so on].
“There is no offense, monk, for a *pārājika*;
there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
Now at that time, a certain monk was telling a story about the hellish realm to a person from hell.
Being terrified, he died.
He felt remorse... [as before] ...
"There is no offense, monk, for one who does not intend death."
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, intending death, spoke a discourse on hell to a person destined for hell.
Terrified, he died... [and so on] ...he was terrified but did not die.
He became anxious... [as before] ...
"There is no offense of a pārājika for you, monk;
there is an offense of a thullaccaya."
Now at that time, the monks of Āḷavī, while performing construction work, were cutting down a tree.
One monk said to another monk:
"Friend, cut it here."
As he was cutting it while standing there, the tree fell over and killed him.
He felt remorse... [as before] ...
"There is no offense, monk, for one who does not intend death."
Now at that time, while the monks of Āḷavī were engaged in construction work, they were cutting down a tree.
A certain monk, with the intention of causing death, said to another monk:
"Friend, cut here, standing right there."
While he was cutting that [tree] standing there, the tree fell and killed him... [etc.
...the tree fell but did not kill him.
He felt remorse... [etc. ...
“There is no offense, monk, for a pārājika;
there is an offense of thullaccaya.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks set fire to a forest grove.
People were burned and died.
They felt remorse... [as before] ...
"There is no offense, monks, for one who does not intend death," he said.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, intending death, set fire to a forest grove.
Some people who were burned died;
some people who were burned did not die.
They became anxious... [as before] ...
"Monks, there is no offense entailing expulsion;
there is an offense of serious transgression."
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu went to an execution ground and said this to an executioner:
"Friend, do not trouble him.
Take his life with a single blow."
“Very well, Bhante,” he said, and with a single blow he deprived him of life.
He felt remorse... [as before]...
“You have committed an offense, monk, a *pārājika*.
Now at that time, a certain monk went to an execution ground and said this to an executioner:
“Friend, do not trouble this man.”
"Kill him with a single blow.
He thought, "I will not do your bidding," and so he deprived him of life.
He felt remorse... [as before] ...
"There is no offense, monk, against a pārājika;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
Now at that time, a certain man whose hands and feet had been cut off was staying at his relatives’ house, surrounded by his kinsmen.
A certain bhikkhu said this to those people:
“Friends, do you wish for this man’s death?”
“Yes, venerable sir, we wish to,” they replied.
“In that case, have them drink buttermilk,” he said.
They had them drink the buttermilk.
He then passed away.
He felt remorse... [as before] ...
"Monk, you have fallen into an offense entailing defeat."
Now at that time, a certain man whose hands and feet had been severed was surrounded by his kinsmen in his family home.
A certain bhikkhunī said this to those people:
"Friends, do you wish for his death?"
“Yes, noble lady, we wish to.
“In that case, give them salted sour gruel to drink.
So they gave them the salted sour gruel to drink.
She then passed away.
She felt remorse...
[as before] ...Then that bhikkhunī reported this matter to the bhikkhunīs.
The bhikkhunīs reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, that bhikkhunī has committed an offense entailing defeat (pārājika)."
The third offense entailing expulsion is finished.
